situation: Launch a driverless ride-hailing service in Austin. The programme is the same one promised as 'over a million robotaxis on the road' in 2020. The remaining work is not making the car drive — it is proving to a regulator, statistically, that it drives more safely than a person.
what_he_actually_did: Launched invite-only in Austin on 22 June 2025 with Tesla staff aboard. Said in October 2025 there would be 500 robotaxis in Austin by year end; revised to about 60 in November.
outcome_detail: By mid-2026 the unsupervised fleet had peaked at 25 vehicles and sat at 20 active, with availability below 20% and a crash rate reported at around nine times worse than human drivers. Dallas and Houston stayed at 3 and 6 vehicles since launch. NHTSA opened investigations after early rides included wrong-side-of-road driving and drop-offs in intersections. Scaling was deferred to an FSD v15 rewrite, pushing any real ramp to late 2026 or 2027.

expect.notes: The engine's largest correction, 3-5x for regulated work, is not enough here and the record says so plainly: a million robotaxis promised for 2020, twenty vehicles running in 2026. This is not the ordinary regulated slip. Where the evidence a regulator needs is statistical -- miles driven, incidents not had -- no amount of urgency compresses it, because the schedule is set by how fast reality can be sampled rather than by how fast anyone works.

decision.decision: Launch an unsupervised robotaxi service in Austin

requirements.text: The fleet must reach 500 vehicles in Austin by year end
The service must run without a human in the driver's seat
Vehicles must demonstrate a lower incident rate than human drivers

steps.name: Run invite-only with staff aboard first
Accumulate the miles the incident-rate claim requires
Wait for the FSD rewrite before launching at all
